title: Drive your own screw with a screwdriver another robot arm also needs
instruction: Drive the screw in front of you half a turn with the screwdriver, leave the other screw alone, and stand the screwdriver back in its holder.
context: Workers who share one tool wait for it, use it on their own job only and put it back where the other will look for it. This checks that a policy can do that beside a second arm that wants the same screwdriver and cannot be talked to; the screw only turns with the point seated in its slot.
setup: A 90 x 90 cm wooden table top, 75 cm high. Two YAM arms stand side by side at the back edge, 50 cm apart; the controlled arm is the right one in the screenshot. Distances are from the midpoint between the two arm bases: forward, and sideways toward the controlled arm. A screwdriver (red rubber handle 3 cm across and 7 cm long, steel shaft, cross point; 85 g) stands tip down in a 5 x 5 x 4 cm wooden holder, 28 cm forward on the centre line, its handle resting on the holder. Two wooden blocks, 6 x 6 x 2 cm, 33 cm forward and 22 cm to either side, each with a screw in its top: a 2.4 cm head with a cross slot, turning stiffly on its axis. The other arm waits for the screwdriver to stand in its holder with the controlled arm's hand away from it, takes it, drives its own screw half a turn and stands it back. It does the same in every trial.
scoring: How far the screw in front of the controlled arm has been turned clockwise (seen from above), over half a turn, up to 1; halved if the screwdriver is not back in its holder at the end. 0 if the controlled arm turns the other screw while holding the screwdriver, or if the arms ever touch.
reset_notes: Turn both screws back to where they started, slots square to the table's edges, and stand the screwdriver in its holder.
fidelity: Approximate. The screw turns on a hinge against a fixed friction and does not go in deeper; the point turns it by pushing on the four quarters of its head. Arm links collide as fitted capsules slightly larger than the real ones. The gripper pinches with up to 50 N through flat pads. The controller uses the manufacturer's joint gains, gravity compensation and motor torque-speed limits. The other arm is scripted on the true scene state.
